units.sourceHTML: Runtime errors #
units.originalInnerHTML: Runtime errors #

units.sourceHTML:
Alas, just fixing all of the “compile-time” errors doesn’t mean your code does
what you want. Your program may still have errors that can’t be detected
statically. Since they can’t be found until your code is run, they’re called
“runtime” errors.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Alas, just fixing all of the “compile-time” errors doesn’t mean your code does
what you want. Your program may still have errors that can’t be detected
statically. Since they can’t be found until your code is run, they’re called
“runtime” errors.

units.sourceHTML:
Most runtime errors come from the VM itself. They arise from code trying to
perform an operation that the VM can’t do. The most common error is a “method
not found” one. If you call a method on an object and its class (and all of its
superclasses) don’t define that method, there’s nothing Wren can do:

units.sourceHTML:
Then it stops executing code. Unlike some other languages, Wren doesn’t keep
plugging away after a runtime error has occurred. A runtime error implies
there’s a bug in your code and it wants to draw your attention to it. To help
you out, it prints a stack trace showing where in the code the error occurred,
and all of the method calls that led to it.

units.sourceHTML: Handling runtime errors #
units.originalInnerHTML: Handling runtime errors #

units.sourceHTML:
Most of the time, runtime errors indicate a bug in your code and the best
solution is to fix the bug. However, sometimes it’s useful to be able to handle
them at, uh, runtime.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Most of the time, runtime errors indicate a bug in your code and the best
solution is to fix the bug. However, sometimes it’s useful to be able to handle
them at, uh, runtime.

units.sourceHTML: To keep the language simpler, Wren does not have exception handling. Instead, it takes advantage of fibers for handling errors. When a runtime error occurs, the current fiber is aborted. Normally, Wren will also abort any fibers that invoked that one, all the way to the main fiber, and then exit the VM.
units.originalInnerHTML: To keep the language simpler, Wren does not have exception handling. Instead, it takes advantage of fibers for handling errors. When a runtime error occurs, the current fiber is aborted. Normally, Wren will also abort any fibers that invoked that one, all the way to the main fiber, and then exit the VM.

units.sourceHTML:
However, you can run a fiber using the ⟦CODE0⟧ method. If a runtime error occurs
in the called fiber, the error is captured and the ⟦CODE1⟧ method returns the
error message as a string.
units.originalInnerHTML: However, you can run a fiber using the try method. If a runtime error occurs in the called fiber, the error is captured and the try method returns the error message as a string.

units.sourceHTML: Failures #
units.originalInnerHTML: Failures #

units.sourceHTML: The last flavor of errors is the highest-level one. All of the above errors indicate bugs—places where the code itself is incorrect. But some errors indicate that the code simply couldn’t accomplish its task for unforeseeable reasons. We’ll call these “failures”.
units.originalInnerHTML: The last flavor of errors is the highest-level one. All of the above errors indicate bugs—places where the code itself is incorrect. But some errors indicate that the code simply couldn’t accomplish its task for unforeseeable reasons. We’ll call these “failures”.

units.sourceHTML:
Consider a program that reads in a string of input from the user and parses it
to a number. Many strings are not valid numbers, so this parsing can fail. The
only way the program could prevent that failure is by validating the string
before its parsed, but validating that a string is a number is pretty much the
same thing as parsing it.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Consider a program that reads in a string of input from the user and parses it
to a number. Many strings are not valid numbers, so this parsing can fail. The
only way the program could prevent that failure is by validating the string
before its parsed, but validating that a string is a number is pretty much the
same thing as parsing it.

units.sourceHTML: For cases like this where failure can occur and the program will want to handle it, fibers and ⟦CODE0⟧ are too coarse-grained to work with. Instead, these operations will indicate failure by returning some sort of error indication.
units.originalInnerHTML: For cases like this where failure can occur and the program will want to handle it, fibers and try() are too coarse-grained to work with. Instead, these operations will indicate failure by returning some sort of error indication.

units.sourceHTML:
For example, a method for parsing a number could return a number on success and
⟦CODE0⟧ to indicate parsing failed. Since Wren is dynamically typed, it’s easy
and natural for a method to return different types of values.
units.originalInnerHTML: For example, a method for parsing a number could return a number on success and null to indicate parsing failed. Since Wren is dynamically typed, it’s easy and natural for a method to return different types of values.
